strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper decomposes GUI agent domain bias into planning-level and grounding-level bias, and designs the pipeline to target each separately. This framing is intuitive, well-illustrated (Fig. 1, Fig. 4), and drives the design choices, making for a coherent narrative.

Strong empirical evidence across settings: results are reported on the full OSWorld benchmark (361 tasks, 10 domains) with three very different agent backbones (Seed-1.8, Qwen3-VL-8B, AgentS3 multi-agent), plus a cross-benchmark transfer to WindowsAgentArena (154 tasks) without retuning. Consistent gains of +4.47 to +7.48 pp on OSWorld and +10.21/+12.46 pp on WAA are convincing evidence of architecture-agnostic generalization.

Well-designed and informative ablations: the dual-channel analysis (Table 1) isolating planning vs grounding contributions, the annotation-pipeline decomposition (Table 4: subtitle-only +2.32, w/o OmniParser +7.52, full +9.11), the retrieval controls (Table 6: full vs title-only vs random), the K ablation (Table 5), and the element-count k sweep (Table 7) collectively isolate which components actually drive the gain.

A genuinely useful negative control: the Watch & Learn-style raw-trajectory ICL baseline (Table 3) scores below the no-annotation baseline, providing direct evidence that the structured, coordinate-free conversion of video trajectories into planning/grounding knowledge—rather than raw retrieved demonstrations—is the source of improvement. This is a nontrivial and informative comparison that strengthens the attribution of the gains.

Human evaluation of the retrieval and annotation pipeline (300 videos, 3 annotators; Fig. 5 and Table 8): reporting 100% precision on GUI-domain classification, 0.867 mean topic score, and 96% precision / 91.6% recall on the Meaningful filter gives credibility to the pipeline quality claims rather than relying solely on downstream task scores.

Practical and reproducible considerations: the paper includes an explicit API-cost analysis (Tables 9–11, $114.6 total for the full benchmark, $0.252 per video) and a concrete comparison against manual annotation-and-fine-tuning pipelines, which makes the practical value proposition concrete.

Honest failure analysis: the supplementary material provides specific failure modes (planning mismatch, grounding mismatch) with detailed examples (Figs. 7–8) and concrete suggested mitigations, which is more than most papers provide and appropriately scopes the claims.

Clarity and presentation: the paper is well-organized, with clear pipeline diagrams and readable tables; design decisions (adaptive top-K, coordinate-free abstraction, reuse-as-reference-not-directive prompting) are explained with motivation.
weaknesses: The pipeline's core components depend heavily on proprietary external LLM APIs (GPT-4.1/-mini for retrieval and GPT-5.1 for annotation), and the reported "training-free, plug-and-play" claim is somewhat undermined by the fact that end-to-end behavior is tied to two specific external models. There is no evaluation of sensitivity to the annotator model beyond a small subset (Table 7b on 50 tasks), and the decomposition into Planning/Grounding is only tested with GPT-5.1 in the main setting. Reproducibility of results is therefore contingent on continued access to these endpoints and on live YouTube retrieval.

The grounding channel's marginal contribution is small relative to planning in the main setting (+0.69–0.80 pp on top of planning in Table 1; +0.41 pp alone on Qwen3 in Table 3). The paper acknowledges this ("positive but modest"), but the abstract's framing of two co-equal knowledge channels somewhat oversells grounding; the balance of the contribution is largely in the planning channel.

A meaningful fraction of the reported improvement appears attributable to transcribed/subtitle text alone rather than to visual video understanding: the subtitle-only ablation (Table 4) already recovers +2.32 pp of +9.11 pp, and the retrieval pipeline itself is explicitly subtitle-driven. While the paper is transparent about this, it does temper the claim that video understanding is the essential ingredient; a text-only RAG baseline (subtitle retrieval + text-derived planning) would clarify the value of the visual annotation stage more sharply.

The retrieval stage is inherently fragile and the paper is candid about this: 17.2% of tasks retrieve no video, retrieved videos can be semantically adjacent but procedurally mismatched (Fig. 7a, Fig. 8a), and live YouTube retrieval raises reproducibility (availability, geo-blocking, rate limits) and legal/ToS/copyright concerns that are not discussed. There is no reported robustness statistic over repeated retrieval runs, though the paper notes Seeds vary in Table 4.

Several design hyperparameters appear heuristic and their robustness is only partially validated: the 10,000 foreground-pixel threshold for keyframe extraction, the 3,000 s duration cap, the top-K ≤ 2 with 0.5 relevance threshold, and the k = 7 element cap. Table 5 shows K = 3 slightly outperforming K = 2 in a few domains, and Table 7a shows the element count k = 5 optimum, but the sensitivity surface is not deeply explored.

The subtitle-driven domain classifier and topic extractor are evaluated with human labels (Fig. 5), but the fact that the labeled pool is pre-filtered by metadata and that false negatives are mostly "visual-only tutorials" suggests the recall numbers may be optimistic relative to the open YouTube distribution.

Absolute success rates remain low (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B goes from 33.9% to 39.7%), and the per-step latency increases (9.5 → 11.6 s). The paper notes grounding reduces the number of steps, which partially compensates, but does not report full end-to-end wall-clock or dollar costs during evaluation for the full benchmark beyond the API-cost tables.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports: "autonomous learning" is used while no learning or parameter update occurs; the system is better described as retrieval-augmented in-context knowledge injection. The distinction matters for framing the contribution's novelty, and the paper does partially address it via the W&L baseline (Table 3), which is the strongest evidence for its claim.

Societal impact is essentially undiscussed. The system relies on scraping third-party tutorial videos and using their content to drive agents, which raises copyright/attribution and platform-terms issues that merit at least a brief discussion, especially given ECCV's repro/attribution expectations.

strengths: The problem is framed cleanly and usefully: domain bias in GUI agents is decomposed into planning-level bias (unknown operation workflows) and grounding-level bias (unfamiliar UI layouts), which is a more actionable framing than a generic 'the model is weak' statement, and it directly motivates the two knowledge channels the method extracts.

The method is training-free and architecture-agnostic, and the evidence for generality is broader than typical: three backbones on OSWorld (Seed-1.8, Qwen3-VL-8B, and the multi-agent AgentS3 with GPT-5.2), plus cross-benchmark transfer to WindowsAgentArena with two backbones without WAA-specific tuning. This is a reasonable basis for the plug-and-play claim.

The ablation set is thoughtful and goes beyond a single headline number: planning vs. grounding channels, number of retrieved videos K, retrieval modes (full vs. title-only vs. random), annotation components (subtitle-only, no-OmniParser), and a same-backbone Watch & Learn-style raw-trajectory ICL control. The latter is a genuinely informative negative result showing raw demos do not substitute for the structured decomposition.

Pipeline stages are audited with human labels (GUI domain classification precision/recall, topic-extraction accuracy, Meaningful-filter precision/recall) rather than asserted, and the appendix provides per-stage API cost accounting and full prompt templates, which aids reproducibility of the prompt-driven parts.

Failure analysis is candid and concrete: two named failure modes (planning mismatch, grounding mismatch) are illustrated with real OSWorld trajectories and wasted-step counts, and the discussion correctly attributes them to retrieval-level semantic/format mismatch and proposes targeted mitigations.

Qualitative example (Fig. 4, GIMP contrast adjustment) is an effective illustration of how planning knowledge redirects the agent from the 'Image' menu to 'Colors', making the claimed mechanism interpretable.
weaknesses: The decisive control is missing. Planning knowledge accounts for ~86-91% of the gain (Sec. 4.2, Tab. 3), and that knowledge is authored by GPT-5.1, a model that very likely already knows these workflows (e.g., GIMP Colors->Brightness-Contrast) from its own prior. No condition injects LLM-authored domain knowledge without any retrieved video, so the experiments do not establish that the improvement comes from the retrieved video content rather than from merely eliciting a stronger annotator model's prior knowledge at test time. This directly threatens the paper's central claim.

Main results carry no uncertainty. Table 1 reports single-run point estimates on a benchmark with known high run-to-run variance, with no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; at +4.47pp on 361 tasks a handful of tasks could account for the effect. The paper further acknowledges Seed-1.8 API instability and malformed outputs, then asserts without evidence that 'the relative improvements from Guide are unaffected'.

'Real-time' is not supported by the reported measurements. The per-task pipeline downloads ~50 YouTube candidates, runs Whisper ASR, MOG2 keyframe extraction, OmniParser, and multiple GPT-5.1 annotation calls, yet only per-step agent latency (9.5 -> 11.6 s, +2.1 s) is reported. There is no end-to-end wall-clock or throughput accounting including retrieval and annotation, which dominates spend (94% of $114.6, $0.252/video). The title/abstract framing overstates practicality.

The advertised innovations contribute modestly at best. Grounding alone gives +0.41pp and the full dual-channel adds only +0.69-0.80pp over planning alone; OmniParser adds +1.59pp on the 120-task subset. The 'fully automated VLM pairwise video annotation pipeline' highlighted in the abstract and contribution (ii)-(iii) is therefore not clearly the source of the reported gains, and the paper does not restructure its claims around the dominant planning channel.

The most directly related retrieval-augmented GUI agent baselines (RAG-GUI [31], KG-RAG [13], OS-Symphony [32]) are discussed in related work but never compared against, despite the paper's claim to be the first to retrieve and process open-web tutorial videos at test time. The only retrieval-side control is a self-constructed Watch & Learn-style ICL variant and title-only/random ranking, which is a weak comparison set for the stated contribution.

Retrieval coverage is only 82.8% (62 of 361 tasks fall back to baseline), and there is no quantitative accounting of harm: the two failure modes in Figs. 7-8 are shown qualitatively with no per-task regression count, so the net benefit/loss trade-off of injecting possibly mismatched knowledge is unmeasured. The Meaningful filter's 53.6% recall on idle no-action frames suggests non-trivial residual contamination of the annotation stream.

Human-evaluation protocol is under-specified for its claim load: three annotators, no inter-annotator agreement statistic (kappa/alpha) for the classification, topic-extraction, or Meaningful-filter studies, and sample sizes (300 videos, 1,227 invalid frames) that are small relative to the general conclusions drawn. In addition, live YouTube dependence makes the retrieval stage non-reproducible by construction, which conflicts with the stated open-science framing, and the abstract's project-page link is empty in the submitted version.
